title: D-B-R
hook: davar is both a word and a thing; midbar, the desert, shares the letters

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tz-L-M: tzelem, the image, one seal and no two faces alike. Your line was the image. Whose face did you look at one second longer? Today closes the week, with a root about words themselves. Day one thousand three hundred eighty-six.

Look back at this week's words. Rachamim, mercy, from the word for womb. Chen, grace. Yada, knowing that means closeness. Banayich read as bonayich, children as builders. Kavod, honor as weight. Tzelem, the image in every face. Six days, and every one of them was a word on a screen and a sound in your ear. Fair question at the end of a week like that: are words just words? Air and ink? Hebrew answers with a root that refuses to keep the two apart. Dalet, bet, resh: D-B-R.
screen: `MERCY, GRACE, KNOWING.` → `BUILDERS, WEIGHT, THE IMAGE.` → `ARE WORDS JUST WORDS?`

segments.voice: D-B-R gives davar, and davar means two things at once: a word, and a thing. Turn it four ways. First, one verse with both. Genesis opens a new scene with Abram this way: "After these things the word of the LORD came unto Abram." Things, there, is devarim. Word is davar. The same root, twice, in one short line, and English needs two different words to carry it. Second, a book named for it. The Hebrew name of Deuteronomy is Devarim, words, from its opening: "These are the words which Moses spoke unto all Israel beyond the Jordan; in the wilderness." Words, and then, a few beats later, wilderness. Third, the wilderness. Wilderness, in that verse, is midbar, and midbar is spelled with a mem in front of the same three letters, D-B-R. The book of Numbers is called Bemidbar in Hebrew, in the wilderness. Some readers hear something in that: the empty place, with nothing in it, is where the words came. The Torah is given in the desert. Fourth, words that make things. The Psalms say, "By the word of the LORD were the heavens made." In Genesis, God says, let there be light, and there is light. In this root, a word is never only air. Once it's said, it's out there, a thing in the world, doing something. A promise is a thing. An insult is a thing. So is a blessing, and so is a sentence of encouragement for a child. This week's words were never just sounds. Each one was meant to become something.
screen: `AFTER THESE THINGS, THE WORD.` · `DEVARIM: THESE ARE THE WORDS.` · `MIDBAR: THE WILDERNESS, SAME LETTERS.` · `BY THE WORD WERE THE HEAVENS MADE.` · then, large: `דָּבָר`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let one word become a deed. Settle, and breathe. Let the week's words pass by once, slowly: mercy, grace, knowing, builders, weight, image. Notice which one stays a little longer than the others. Take that one. Now give it a body. If it's mercy, who could use some today? If it's weight, whose words will you let land? Picture the deed, small and specific: a call, a note, a door held open. Hold the picture. If you pray, you can carry the word into the quiet. The bell holds the time.
D-B-R. Dalet, bet, resh: davar, a word and a thing at once; the letters inside midbar, the wilderness. Today's word.
Your line: words are things. Today, do the deed you pictured, and before you sleep, check that the word became a thing. Day one thousand three hundred eighty-six.

howItsDone: Jews call the fifth book of the Torah Devarim, words, and the fourth Bemidbar, in the wilderness, from words near their openings; Jewish ethics treats speech seriously, with whole bodies of law about promises, vows and harmful talk.

myth: davar can mean both a word and a thing
Genesis uses the root for both in one line: after these things, the word.
the Hebrew name of Deuteronomy means laws
it's Devarim, words, from "These are the words which Moses spoke."
midbar, wilderness, has nothing in common with davar
midbar is a mem in front of the same letters, D-B-R.

fork.setup: Genesis: "after these things the word of the LORD came unto Abram." in Hebrew, what are "things" and "word"?
options: the same word, just spelled backward.
fork.reveal: devarim, things, and davar, word. Hebrew keeps the word and the thing in one root.

original.note: Hebrew: a word, a thing, a matter.

trapdoor: what you thought: words are just sounds, and things are things.
what it means: in Hebrew, davar means both a word and a thing.
what a scholar hears: Genesis 15:1 uses the root twice, and Deuteronomy 1:1 sets devarim beside midbar.
